_why: Captured from main at 862d4b3, before courses began covering topics through a catalog, and re-captured once since. A generic student is promised that nothing moved; this is the promise, written down. smoke.mjs compares against it. If a line here has to change, that change is a decision about generic students and belongs in its own commit with its own reason.
_moved: Re-captured 2026-10-08, when the route comparison offer landed on the Route. Three lines were ADDED to both reveal strings and nothing was removed or altered; explain, coverage and both figures lines were byte-identical and are carried over unchanged. That diff was read line by line before this file was rewritten, because a snapshot updated without reading the diff is a snapshot that has stopped checking anything.
_labels: The sheet’s parcel labels are NOT in this text. fitSheetLabels() chooses between the full name, the short name, a rotated name and nothing by MEASURING the rendered width, and smoke.mjs blocks Google Fonts on purpose — so the label a parcel ends up with depends on whichever fallback face the machine running the check happens to have. That is a property of the font, not of Waypoint, and a check that fails on somebody else’s laptop for it is worse than no check. The figures line below carries the coverage figure and all nineteen topic states, which is what the labels were standing in for.
_terms: The test-term question is not in this text either, for the same kind of reason one step removed. It offers the next seven MCAT seatings, so its chips read "Spring 2027" through "Spring 2029" today and something else after the next January: a snapshot of them would start failing on a calendar page turn rather than on a change anybody made. smoke.mjs hides .cmp-term for the reading. The question has its own test, where the date it is run on is the thing being checked.

screens.junior/coverage:
Back

Your route

The Waypoint Coverage Model.

The MCAT is 230 questions, and AAMC publishes exactly what is in them: 59 on biology and biochemistry, 59 on chemistry and physics, 59 on psychology and sociology, 53 on reading — and a stated mix of disciplines inside each one.

The Coverage Model maps premed coursework onto that structure: each course to the MCAT topics it teaches, each topic to its discipline's real share of the exam. AAMC publishes what the exam contains. Nobody publishes which of your classes covers it. That mapping is what turns I took Biochem into a number.

Every figure comes from AAMC's own published data, the arithmetic is written out, and you can recheck the whole thing with a calculator. Complex enough to be right. Simple enough that you can check it.

See the whole derivation

What the number means

It is the share of MCAT content your coursework covers — not the share of questions you would get right, and not a prediction of how you will score.

Courses map to 77% of MCAT content. The other 23% is CARS — a reading skill, not a topic to unlock, and the one figure here that is simply AAMC's: 53 of the 230 questions. Because all four sections count equally toward your score, CARS is about a quarter of it.

Percentages below are Waypoint's own content weights — an estimate of how much MCAT material each topic accounts for. They are not AAMC question counts.

Which classes do I still need?

Required by most med schools: a year each of Biology, General Chemistry, Organic Chemistry, and Physics (all with labs), plus English and a math or statistics course.

Before the MCAT: all of the above plus Biochemistry — it's heavily tested, so finish it before you sit the exam.

MCAT-tested but not required for admission: Psychology and Sociology (together ~18% of the exam).

English isn't tracked here (it's not MCAT content), but most schools require two semesters.
